methodological_questions: Measuring causal impact of play types
Handling confounding in sequential basketball data
Statistical methods for sequence modeling in basketball
Controlling for game state and personnel in play analysis

historical_evidence.finding: Play types and players have a real downstream (opponent next-PPP) component beyond direct PPP. 4/8 PTs downstream real: CUT Ext 1.658 (supp +0.0220), TRANSITION 1.509 (+0.0145), SPOT_UP 1.303 (+0.0124), POST_UP 1.127 (+0.0194).

After the opponent runs play type X, the next offensive play type Y scores above Y's unconditional H2 baseline, and every PT has a defensive aftershock. [APPA-049] A2 aftershock 8/8 PTs replicate all-games and playoffs (CUT +0.119 n=21,398 / PO +0.131 n=1,145 through TRANSITION +0.135 n=26,262 / +0.126 n=1,529).

Running play type X raises the same team's next 1-5 possession PPP vs a matched baseline (action memory). Global horizons: DRIVE/SPOT_UP/TRANSITION=5; others 0 (PNR/CUT/POST_UP/PUTBACK). SPOT_UP lag-1 lift +0.027 ctrl_p=0.0000. Within-team: all horizons 0 except SPOT_UP horizon(all)=1; PNR lag-1 within_team_lift=-0.0218.

Play-type actions have decaying cross-possession memory (lag-1 effect >= lag-2; not just score margin or team quality). FAIL decay-sanity: DRIVE lifts +0.015,+0.020,+0.018,+0.021,+0.020 (flat). Within-team: DRIVE lag-1 +0.015 to -0.002. Cohen d ~0.01-0.03; p~0 from n>150k. Callable play-type horizons = 0.

Play-type PPP differences are real efficiency, not labeling/foul artifacts. OTHER: 36% end in fouls, PPP inflated (FOUL_BUCKET). DRIVE: 12pp below foul benchmark (FOUL_LEAK). PNR shows 22% foul rate. Only 335 of 50,668 possessions (0.7%) map to a real play type via initiation_type.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Measuring downstream effects (opponent next-PPP) for players and some play types.
failed_approaches.why: Downstream effects are small (~0.01-0.02 PPP) relative to direct PPP gaps; player list is mostly non-FINDING after BH.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Measuring persistent impact score lag curves (own-sequence lags).
failed_approaches.why: Flat non-decaying global lifts disappear after team-season demeaning; remaining within-team memory is essentially none except SPOT_UP lag-1.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Measuring persistent impact score level 1 gate for decaying cross-possession memory.
failed_approaches.why: Flat non-decaying lifts collapse under within-team baseline; team-quality confound.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Identifying superstar sequential suppression from opponent play.
failed_approaches.why: No multiplicity correction; n_after is 32-95 for several PUTBACK cells vs thousands of baseline possessions.
Rank-1 deltas mostly within 1-2 SE with no multiple-comparison control; OTHER artifact flagged in doc.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Assessing season stability of top suppressors.
failed_approaches.why: Only 2/30 stars meet the 75% same-top-suppressor stability rule.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Play-type labeling audit for OTHER/DRIVE foul leakage.
failed_approaches.why: OTHER PPP inflated by 36% foul endings; DRIVE 12pp below foul benchmark; initiation_type maps 0.7%.

evidence_establishes: Defensive aftershocks (opponent next-possession PPP) exist for all 8 major play types after the opponent runs a play, with impacts around +0.12 PPP (FAM:SF07).

Some offensive play types (CUT, TRANSITION, SPOT_UP, POST_UP) are associated with small but 'real' downstream opponent next-PPP effects when *our* team runs them, in the range of +0.01 to +0.02 PPP (FAM:SF-APPS-075).

Naive global measurements of 'own-sequence lags' (a team's play affecting its *own* subsequent PPP) are often artifacts driven by team quality or other confounds and largely disappear after proper controls (FAM:SF-APPS-073, FAM:SF-CHT-029).

The reliability and accuracy of play-type labels, especially for 'OTHER' and 'DRIVE', can be problematic and lead to inflated or deflated PPP figures due to foul-ending rates or poor initiation type mapping (FAM:SF-CHT-025).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether the observed opponent next-possession PPP effects are 'large enough' to drive AVOID labels, as no link between these effects and the AVOID labeling system has been established or quantified.
The causal mechanisms behind the observed sequential effects, beyond statistical association.
The full extent and magnitude of 'own-sequence lags' for all play types after robust controls for all potential confounders.
The stability of sequential suppression effects across seasons for individual players (FAM:SF-APPA-058 found little stability).
own_inferences: The research question combines two distinct types of sequential effects: defensive aftershocks (our play affecting opponent's next possession) and offensive action memory (our play affecting our own next possession).

The phrase 'large enough to drive AVOID labels' implies a specific threshold or causal relationship to an existing labeling system, which is not directly addressed by historical findings on effect magnitudes alone.

The data available includes play-by-play, which is suitable for reconstructing possession sequences and calculating PPP, and derived play-type possession records, which are essential for identifying 'play X'.
uncertainties: The definition and threshold for 'large enough' to drive AVOID labels are undefined.
The specific methodology for deriving 'AVOID labels' is not provided, making it difficult to assess how sequential PPP effects would interact with it.
The extent to which the existing play-type labeling (from the derived records) is robust against the issues identified in FAM:SF-CHT-025 (foul leakage, poor initiation mapping).

historical_effect.explanation: The historical evidence significantly changed the assessment of 'own-sequence lags' from potentially real to likely artifactual without rigorous controls. It also highlighted the small magnitude of direct downstream effects (opponent next-PPP) for *our* plays (SF-APPS-075) compared to the larger 'defensive aftershock' effects after *opponent* plays (SF07), suggesting the 'large enough' criterion for AVOID labels might be challenging for the former. Furthermore, it underscored the critical importance of controlling for confounding and the potential for labeling artifacts, which necessitate a more robust design than initially implied by the question.

blocking_constraints.text: Sequential effects are highly susceptible to confounding by team quality, game state, score margin, and personnel, as shown by the 'artifact' status of global lag effects in prior studies (FAM:SF-APPS-073, FAM:SF-CHT-029).

The reliability of play-type labels has been questioned (FAM:SF-CHT-025), with issues like foul leakage and low mapping rates for 'initiation_type', which could impact the accuracy of 'play X' identification.

The frequency of specific play-type sequences might lead to small sample sizes for certain combinations, affecting statistical power, especially for player-specific or nuanced sequential effects (FAM:SF-APPA-050, FAM:SF-APPA-058).
The 'AVOID labels' are a derived outcome, and their derivation process needs to be clearly defined to understand how sequential PPP effects might 'drive' them. Without this, the link is untestable.

prior_work.summary: Historical work has established the existence of small downstream effects on opponent next-PPP after a team's play, and significant 'defensive aftershock' effects after an opponent's play. However, strong evidence suggests 'own-sequence lags' (action memory) are mostly artifacts without rigorous controls. The question's link to 'AVOID labels' is novel and not addressed. Furthermore, play-type labeling quality is a known risk.

risks.text: The impact of play type X on subsequent PPP is highly confounded by team quality, opponent quality, game state (score, clock), personnel on the floor, and other preceding events not captured by 'play X'. Robust controls (e.g., team-season demeaning, matched baselines, regression with extensive covariates) are essential.

The 'play type' labels from the derived possession records might suffer from inaccuracies or biases, as indicated by historical findings on foul leakage and poor initiation mapping (FAM:SF-CHT-025). This could lead to misattribution of effects.

While overall possession counts are large, specific sequences of 'play X' followed by opponent possessions or particular 'own-sequence lags' might have insufficient sample sizes to detect small effects with adequate power, especially if segmented by player or specific game situations.
The base rate of certain play types or sequences might be low, making it difficult to establish statistically significant effects or generalize findings.

If effects are tested across multiple play types, players, or lag horizons, controlling for multiple comparisons will be crucial to avoid spurious findings, a known issue in prior work (FAM:SF-APPA-050, FAM:SF-APPM-022).

The 'AVOID labels' are a derived outcome. The criteria for these labels must be explicitly defined. If they already incorporate some form of sequential PPP, the research question becomes circular or tautological. If they don't, linking a small PPP effect to a categorical label threshold requires careful justification.

design.estimand: The causal effect of running specific offensive play type X on: 1) the opponent's next possession Points Per Possession (PPP_opp_T+1), and 2) the team's own next possession Points Per Possession (PPP_own_T+1), adjusted for relevant confounders. The secondary estimand is to quantify the magnitude of these effects relative to a defined threshold for 'AVOID labels'.
design.unit: Possession (an offensive sequence ending in a shot, turnover, or foul, derived from play-by-play data).
design.sample: All NBA regular season and playoff possessions from 2022-23 to 2025-26 (partial for 25-26 playoffs, complete for 25-26 regular season). Minimum `n_after` for each play type X will be set to 1000 for primary analysis, higher for player-level analysis. Data will be filtered for possessions where 'play X' is clearly identified and not an 'OTHER' or high-foul-rate play type.
design.power: Target a minimum detectable effect size (MDES) of 0.05 PPP for opponent next-possession PPP and 0.02 PPP for own next-possession PPP, with 80% power at alpha=0.05. Power analysis will be conducted based on observed variance in PPP and expected frequencies of play types. Small effects (e.g., 0.01-0.02 PPP) may require larger sample sizes or be deemed practically insignificant.
design.controls: A difference-in-differences approach or a regression model with extensive controls will be used. Controls must include: team-season fixed effects (to address team quality confounding), opponent quality, game state (score differential, time remaining), current lineup, preceding play outcome (e.g., made/missed shot, turnover), and whether the possession immediately followed a dead ball. For own-sequence lags, a matched baseline (e.g., propensity score matching or exact matching on game state and team characteristics) will be crucial, similar to successful approaches in prior work to mitigate artifactual findings.
design.falsification: 1. Test for effects at lag horizons beyond 1 (e.g., lag 2, 3) to check for decaying memory; flat or increasing lifts beyond lag 1 would suggest confounding. 2. Conduct placebo tests by randomizing 'play X' labels within games or teams and ensuring no significant effects are detected. 3. Test for effects of 'play X' on outcomes that should not be affected (e.g., opponent foul rate on non-shooting plays).
design.multiplicity: Adjust p-values for multiple comparisons using a method like Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR) or Bonferroni correction, especially when testing across multiple play types or players. Clearly state the family-wise error rate or false discovery rate controlled.
design.decision_rule: The research question will be considered 'supported' if statistically significant (p < alpha_adjusted) and practically meaningful effects (e.g., >0.05 PPP for opponent next-PPP, >0.02 PPP for own-next PPP) are found for a substantial number of relevant play types, after robust controls, and a clear, justifiable link to 'AVOID labels' can be demonstrated. Otherwise, it will be 'rejected' (if adequately powered null), 'artifact' (if effects disappear under controls), or 'untestable' (if the link to AVOID labels cannot be established).
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25 regular seasons and playoffs (complete); NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete) and playoffs (partial as of 2026-06-19). Derived play-type possession records and play-by-play from NBA stats API.

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

messages.content:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-19, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

  }
}
